title: F2AI Focus | What Stability AI’s Founder-CEO Exit Means for Other AI Startups
summary: Multiple outlets reported that Stability AI founder and CEO Emad Mostaque has stepped down from all company roles. In a Friday-evening press release, Stability AI said Mostaque is leaving to “pursue decentralized AI,” and that he is also resigning from the board.
author: Unique Research
html:
Unique Research · F2AI Focus · March 29, 2024

Multiple outlets reported that Stability AI founder and CEO Emad Mostaque has stepped down from all company roles. In a Friday-evening press release, Stability AI said Mostaque is leaving to “pursue decentralized AI,” and that he is also resigning from the board.

The board named COO Shan Shan Wong and CTO Christian Laforte interim co-CEOs while it searches for a successor. Chair Jim O’Shaughnessy thanked Mostaque for “leadership and tireless commitment to Stability AI and the open-source movement.”

“Stability” was not yet stable — and the founding team is already leaving

As a closely watched AI unicorn, Stability AI is best known for the open-source text-to-image model Stable Diffusion, which helped make it one of the world’s leading open generative-AI companies and drew large developer and enterprise interest.

Stable Diffusion powers many text-to-image tools. Weeks earlier Stability released its latest model, Stable Cascade, as a GitHub option for researchers. In December it also launched paid memberships for commercial model use to fund research.

Despite the “Stability” name, the company under Mostaque lived through turbulent years. His exit followed a Forbes report that Stability was in trouble and that other key developers had already quit — including three of the five researchers who originally created Stable Diffusion.

Executive churn was only one problem. Bloomberg reported that a major investor last autumn pressed Mostaque to resign as cash reserves fell. Reports say Stability has burned through most of the roughly $100M it raised, with monthly burn recently cited at about $8M.

Former employees say the firm is a shadow of its peak — recruiting described as a “hollow shell” — and that before Mostaque left amid high ongoing costs, legal issues, and shrinking resources, the company had entered a “death spiral.” Bloomberg sources last year argued the trouble was more mismanagement than competition.

A crypto entrepreneur by background, Mostaque ran the AI startup in a crypto-style register: frequent confrontation with big institutions and heavy hype. Insiders say his internal control was strong; ex-leaders call the style chaotic — yanking people off one project to rush another. One example: last summer, despite a backlog of customer-support tickets, staff were pulled off those queues.

As CEO he also made claims Bloomberg flagged as unrealistic. At a July Bloomberg event, asked about gender and racial bias in image generators like Stable Diffusion, he said the company was working with “multiple governments” on models tuned to each country’s norms. Three people who worked there said they saw no evidence of such government agreements during their tenure.

His personal résumé also carried disputed items: before founding Stability AI in late 2020, the British–Bangladeshi executive had a history of overstatement — from a claimed Oxford master’s degree to a fabricated “strategic partnership” with Amazon.

Is Microsoft becoming the new AI oligarch — always the class representative?

As Stability’s leadership shifted, so did another star AI startup: Inflection AI. Co-founders Mustafa Suleyman and Karén Simonyan, plus several colleagues, moved in one of Satya Nadella–led Microsoft’s stranger talent deals.

Suleyman will lead Microsoft’s new consumer AI unit, Microsoft AI, as EVP and CEO of Microsoft AI, reporting to Nadella; Simonyan joins as chief scientist.

Beyond hiring the founders, Microsoft paid about $620M for exclusive rights to Inflection’s AI models, plus roughly $30M more so Inflection waives legal claims tied to the mass hire. UCL science-and-technology studies professor Jack Stilgoe: “AI startups are panicking about how to compete with emerging (generative) AI oligopolies.”

The newly departed Mostaque also quickly linked up with Nadella — posting a selfie from a video call with the Microsoft CEO, with tongue-in-cheek lines such as “He is above, below and around us” and “In Satya we trust (because at this rate we’ll kinda have to).”

Mostaque has long argued AI should not belong to a single entity. In practice the frontier remains tightly held by leaders. OpenAI co-founder Elon Musk has repeatedly attacked OpenAI for abandoning its open, non-profit origins for a closed, profit-driven firm controlled by big tech — with Microsoft and Nadella as the main enablers.

Is Big Tech monopoly of the AI market inevitable?

Early this year the drama of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s firing and rehiring looked like a board fight; underneath was OpenAI–Microsoft. Though the non-profit structure nominally put the board in control, Microsoft’s concern and the ensuing employee revolt forced Altman’s return.

Microsoft did not acquire OpenAI outright — in part to avoid antitrust heat. That relationship is only one slice of a growing AI oligopoly. A recent paper by UC Berkeley’s Tejas Narechania and Vanderbilt’s Ganesh Sitaraman maps concentration across the AI supply chain: Nvidia supplies most chips AI development needs; Amazon, Google, and Microsoft dominate the cloud that stores training data; AI firms race to capture as much content and data as possible. Almost every major tech firm and its executives are cross-linked. A small circle keeps the gate to AGI tightly shut.

What should startup AI companies take from this?

Stability AI was emblematic: its rise showed GenAI’s potential; its burn now shows how brutal the race is — a popular new technology alone is nowhere near enough.

a16z partners still call this a dual opportunity for startups: invent products on new architectures, and exploit big-company transition fragility. Reality for most AI startups is pressure on both flanks — build capability, find stable customers and a business model, and resist Big Tech squeeze.

Lessons from Stability’s story:

  1. Clear business positioning. Stability shipped a strong Stable Diffusion yet failed to build a broad user base; Midjourney, often seen as less “tech-heavy,” won users with experience. Innovation must meet demand and market fit.
  2. A durable commercial model. Costs near $8M/month with far lower revenue is unsustainable. Technology must become payable, ongoing service.
  3. Turn content into service. Pure tech products rarely cover cost in AI; personalized, continuous expert-grade service is how models become businesses.

Companies that manage all three are already lucky. More startups watch technical edges get crushed overnight by a big lab’s next release — as with Sora versus Runway and Pika.

Building a profitable AI company faces costs typical startups do not: GPU purchase/rent, widening talent gaps, high salaries, expensive APIs and hosting — burn can runaway fast. Many AI startups have huge potential; lasting success still needs flexibility, cost control, a clear model, and a moat Big Tech cannot casually kill.

7 CN images; attach on ingest. Column intro block omitted as non-editorial.

— END —
